hints: Rewrite cosecant and cotangent using sine and cosine, then simplify with double-angle identities.
Use $1-\cos2\theta=2\sin^2\theta$ and $\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ to obtain the right side.
walkthrough:
Express $\csc 2\theta$ and $\cot 2\theta$ in terms of $\sin 2\theta$ and $\cos 2\theta$:
$$\csc 2\theta - \cot 2\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sin 2\theta} - \dfrac{\cos 2\theta}{\sin 2\theta} = \dfrac{1 - \cos 2\theta}{\sin 2\theta}$$

Cancel the common factor of $2\sin\theta$ (for $\sin\theta \ne 0$):
$$\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \tan\theta$$
Therefore:
$$\csc 2\theta - \cot 2\theta \equiv \tan\theta$$
This completes the proof.

hints: Replace the integrand by $\tan\theta$ using part (a).
Use $\int\tan\theta\,d\theta=-\ln|\cos\theta|$ and apply the limits $\pi/4$ and $\pi/3$.
Insert the exact cosine values, then combine the logarithms to show the stated result.
walkthrough:
Use the trigonometric identity established in part (a) to rewrite the definite integral:
$$\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} (\csc 2\theta - \cot 2\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta = \int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \tan\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta$$

Subtract the lower limit value from the upper limit value:
$$\ln 2 - \dfrac{1}{2}\ln 2 = \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)\ln 2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\ln 2$$
This completes the proof.
